477.title: Masei: one date of death (Numbers 33:38)
477.hook: the only death the Torah dates exactly is Aaron's
477.howItsDone: The yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death by the Hebrew calendar, is commonly marked by lighting a candle that burns for a full day, saying the mourner's Kaddish, and often giving charity in the person's memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masei, the journeys, with every stop on the road named, even the forgettable ones. Your line was every stop counts.

Some dates live in a phone calendar. Others arrive on their own, without a reminder: the week a parent died, the day the house burned, an anniversary nobody else seems to remember. They come back every year, whether anyone writes them down or not. In the middle of the long list of campsites, the Torah suddenly stops. Between one station and the next, it pauses for a death. And it does something rare: it gives the exact date.
screen: `DATES THAT ARRIVE ON THEIR OWN.` → `THE LIST STOPS FOR A DEATH.` → `THE EXACT DATE.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase: Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the Lord's command and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel came out of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month. Then: Aaron was a hundred and twenty-three years old when he died on Mount Hor. Year, month, day and age. That is rare. Even Moses' death, at the end of Deuteronomy, comes without a date. The rabbis later worked out a traditional date for Moses, the seventh of Adar, by calculating from other verses, but the Torah itself doesn't say. For Aaron, it does. The fifth month in the Torah's counting is the month later called Av, so Aaron died on the first of Av. The Torah had already told the story of his death back in Chukat; here it marks the day. Why? The text doesn't explain. But Jewish life has kept the instinct. The anniversary of a death, by the Hebrew calendar, is called a yahrzeit, a Yiddish word meaning a year's time. On that day the custom is to light a candle that burns for a whole day, say the mourner's Kaddish, give charity, and sometimes study in the person's memory. Some communities mark Aaron's own yahrzeit on the first of Av. A death is not just an event in the story; it's a day that comes back, and here the Torah marks the day.
screen: `THE FORTIETH YEAR, FIFTH MONTH, FIRST DAY.` · `NO DATE FOR MOSES IN THE TORAH.` · `THE FIRST OF AV.` · `YAHRZEIT: A YEAR'S TIME.`

478.title: Masei: cities of refuge (Numbers 35:9–15)
478.hook: six cities where one who killed by accident could flee
478.howItsDone: The cities of refuge are read in the portion of Masei in midsummer, and their laws are studied in the Talmud tractate Makkot, which describes the roads, signs and care for those who fled there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah paused its list of journeys to give one exact date of death, Aaron's, on the first of Av. Your line was dates are remembered.

A second of distraction on a wet road. A ladder that wasn't tied down. An accident that ends a life, and nobody meant it. In the ancient world, that wasn't the end of the story. A relative of the person who died might come looking for blood. The Torah even has a name for him: the avenger of blood. It doesn't pretend that anger away. But as the people stand at the edge of the land, it sets aside six cities, built for the person who did the worst thing they never meant to do.
screen: `AN ACCIDENT, AND NOBODY MEANT IT.` → `A RELATIVE COMES LOOKING.` → `SIX CITIES SET ASIDE.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase: when you cross the Jordan, choose cities to be cities of refuge, so that someone who kills a person by accident can flee there. Six in all: three east of the Jordan, three in the land of Canaan. They're open to everyone: to Israelites, and to the stranger and the settler living among them. The Hebrew is ir miklat, a city of refuge, of shelter. There the person was safe from the avenger, and would have a proper trial. If the death was found to be an accident, they lived in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest, then could go home. The rabbis made this law humane in surprising detail. The Talmud says the roads to the cities had to be kept in good repair, and at every crossroads a sign read refuge, refuge, so a frightened person running for their life would never take a wrong turn. The cities needed water and markets, and had to be neither too small nor too crowded. If a student had to flee there, the Talmud says, his teacher went with him, so he wouldn't be cut off from learning. And the mothers of the high priests, it says, brought food and clothing to the people in the cities, so they wouldn't pray for the high priest to die. None of this pretends the death didn't happen. The person still lived away from home for as long as that high priest lived. But a mistake didn't have to end in another death. There was a road, signposted, to somewhere safe.

segments.voice: Think of someone who hurt you, or others, without meaning to: a careless word, an honest mistake with real consequences. Let the part of you that wants them to pay be there, then ask whether you could leave a road to refuge open for them, not pretending it didn't happen, but not chasing them either.

479.title: Masei: the land is shared (Numbers 35:33–34)
479.hook: bloodshed pollutes the land in which God dwells
479.howItsDone: These verses close the laws of homicide in Masei, read in midsummer, and Jewish law draws from related verses the principle of bal tashchit, avoiding needless destruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masei's six cities of refuge, with signs at every crossroads reading refuge, refuge. Your line was a place of refuge. Today, the two verses that close those laws.

Some places hold what happened in them. People stop wanting to live in a house after something terrible happens there. A street corner gets flowers and candles for years. Somehow, even without explaining it, people feel that ground remembers. After the cities of refuge, the Torah ends its laws about killing with two verses that say exactly that. They aren't about the one who killed, or the family who grieves. They're about the land itself, and who else lives on it.
screen: `A HOUSE NOBODY WANTS TO LIVE IN.` → `FLOWERS ON A STREET CORNER.` → `THE GROUND REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Here are the verses, mostly in paraphrase. Don't pollute the land you live in, the Torah says, because blood pollutes the land, and the land can't be cleansed of blood shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it. Then the last line: don't defile the land you live in, where I dwell, and in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the children of Israel." Notice the turn. It isn't only your land. Someone else lives in it too. In Leviticus, God says it even more plainly: the land is Mine, and you are like strangers and settlers with Me. Not owners: tenants, sharing a house with its owner. So violence isn't just a crime between two families; it stains a shared home. An early midrash says bloodshed defiles the land and causes the Divine Presence to withdraw from it. The chapter itself, a few verses earlier, refuses any ransom for a murderer's life: no payment buys a way out. And the idea that the land itself can be harmed, and that people answer for it, has stayed in Jewish thought. Later teachers drew from other verses a law against needless destruction, called bal tashchit, starting with not cutting down fruit trees in war. The land is shared: with each other, with those who come after, and, the Torah says, with God.
screen: `BLOOD POLLUTES THE LAND.` · `I DWELL IN THE MIDST.` · `THE LAND IS MINE: YOU ARE TENANTS.` · `BAL TASHCHIT: DON'T DESTROY NEEDLESSLY.`

480.title: Numbers close: chazak
480.hook: the people stand on the plains of Moab, at the edge of the land
480.howItsDone: When the last verse of Numbers is read in synagogue, usually at the end of the double portion Matot-Masei in midsummer, the congregation calls out chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek, and the reader repeats it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masei's last law: blood pollutes the land, because God dwells in the midst of it. Your line was the land is shared. Today, the book of Numbers ends.

The night before a move, the boxes are packed and the rooms echo. You're not in the old life anymore, and not yet in the new one. The book of Numbers ends right there. It began in the wilderness of Sinai, at the foot of the mountain, with a count of the men, name by name. It ends on the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan, across from Jericho. The river is right there. Nobody has crossed it yet.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE A MOVE.` → `IT BEGAN AT SINAI.` → `IT ENDS ON THE PLAINS OF MOAB.`

segments.voice: The very last story in Numbers is a small one, and it brings back old friends. The leaders of the tribe of Manasseh come to Moses with a worry about Zelophehad's daughters, the five sisters who won the right to inherit. If they marry into another tribe, the land goes with them, and the tribe's share shrinks. Moses answers, in paraphrase: the tribe speaks right too. The daughters may marry whomever they choose, as long as it's within their father's tribe. And they do. The book ends with a fair compromise, both sides heard. Then the final verse, in paraphrase: these are the commandments and the laws that the Lord commanded through Moses to the children of Israel, on the plains of Moab, by the Jordan, at Jericho. The book opened with a census of a generation that left Egypt. Nearly all of that generation is gone now, through the spies, the rebellions, and the long years of walking. A second census, back in Pinchas, counted their children. Miriam and Aaron have died. Moses knows he won't cross. The people on the plains of Moab were mostly born in the desert, or were children when they left. So when the reader in synagogue finishes the last verse of Numbers, the congregation calls out the words said at the end of each book of the Torah: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another. Here it lands differently from the end of Leviticus. This time, everyone is standing at a river.
screen: `THE TRIBE SPEAKS RIGHT TOO.` · `ON THE PLAINS OF MOAB.` · `A NEW GENERATION AT THE RIVER.` · `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, V'NITCHAZEK.`

segments.voice: Let a few moments from this wilderness book come back: counted by name, the priestly blessing, the fish they missed, the spies who felt like grasshoppers, Korach, the rock, a donkey who saw first, five sisters, every stop on the road. 481.title: These are the words
481.hook: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell speech, retelling forty years
481.tomorrow: Devarim: the man of few words speaks
481.howItsDone: Deuteronomy is read in synagogue from midsummer to early fall, ending on Simchat Torah, and its first portion, Devarim, is read on the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, or on the day itself when Tisha B'Av falls on the Sabbath and the fast is postponed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Numbers closed on the plains of Moab, with chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek. Your line was at the edge. Today, a new book.

Near the end of a life, some people want to tell their story. Not the whole thing, start to finish, but the parts that mattered, told their way, to the people who'll go on without them. Grandparents do it at the kitchen table. Teachers do it in a last lecture. The fifth book of the Torah is that kind of telling. Tradition says Moses has only weeks left. The people are camped across from the land he will never enter. And he begins to talk.
screen: `THE PARTS THAT MATTERED.` → `A FEW WEEKS LEFT.` → `AND HE BEGINS TO TALK.`

segments.voice: The book opens, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan." In Hebrew, Eleh ha-devarim. These are the words. And that gives the book its Hebrew name: Devarim, words. The English name, Deuteronomy, comes from the old Greek translation and means something like second law, from a phrase inside the book about a copy of the teaching. The rabbis sometimes called it Mishneh Torah, the repetition of the Torah. Both names catch something. Much of what Moses says, you've heard before: the Ten Commandments, the spies, the golden calf, laws about festivals and justice. But this time it's not the narrator telling it. It's Moses, mostly speaking in his own voice, to a generation that was too young to remember, or wasn't born yet. And memory isn't a recording. When Moses retells the spies, for example, he says it was the people who first asked to send them, a detail that isn't in the version in Numbers. This is the story as he lived it, and wants them to keep it. The book opens on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year. By the end of it, Moses has died. Jewish tradition counts the time between as only a few weeks. So the whole book is a farewell: one long last conversation. A new part of the path begins here, portion by portion through Moses' last words. Before anything else, notice the frame. The final thing the Torah gives is a person speaking to the people he loves.
screen: `ELEH HA-DEVARIM: THESE ARE THE WORDS.` · `DEUTERONOMY: A SECOND TELLING.` · `THE STORY AS MOSES LIVED IT.` · `ONE LONG LAST CONVERSATION.`

482.title: Devarim: the man of few words speaks (Deuteronomy 1:1)
482.hook: the one who said he was no man of words now speaks a whole book
482.howItsDone: Jewish communities begin reading Deuteronomy in the synagogue each summer with the portion Devarim, which is always read on the Sabbath just before Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devarim: words, and a whole book of Moses' farewell. Your line was last words matter. Today, a look at who is doing the talking.

Go back forty years, to a bush on fire in the desert. God tells a shepherd to go to Pharaoh, and the shepherd argues. In the old Jewish translation of Exodus he says, "I am not a man of words." He's slow of speech, he says, slow of tongue. Send someone else. God sends his brother Aaron along to do the talking. Now jump to the edge of the Jordan. The shepherd is an old man of a hundred and twenty. And the book that opens today is almost entirely him, talking, speech after speech.
screen: `I AM NOT A MAN OF WORDS.` → `AARON DOES THE TALKING.` → `FORTY YEARS LATER: A WHOLE BOOK.`

segments.voice: The book begins: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel." In Hebrew, eleh ha-devarim. Devarim means words. The rabbis heard the irony right away. A midrash, in Deuteronomy Rabbah, sets the two verses side by side. At the bush, the Hebrew is lo ish devarim anochi, not a man of devarim. Here, eleh ha-devarim. The same word, forty years apart. Before, he couldn't speak. Now he speaks a whole book. What changed? The midrash's answer is that living with the Torah healed his tongue. Another way to hear it: forty years happened. He led a people who complained, he lost his sister and his brother, he broke tablets and carved new ones. Someone who has carried that much has something to say, and maybe stops worrying whether it comes out beautifully. And look at who he's speaking to: a generation that mostly wasn't there for the start of it, their parents having died in the wilderness. The man who once asked for someone else to do the talking is now the one who remembers out loud for everyone. He doesn't need to be polished. He needs to have been there. So the book of words belongs to the man who once had none. They didn't come from talent. They came from time.

483.title: Devarim: small and great alike (Deuteronomy 1:17)
483.hook: judges must hear the small as the great and fear no one
483.howItsDone: Jewish law holds judges to equal care for every case regardless of its value or the parties' standing, and the Talmud's rule that a penny case is as precious as a fortune is still cited in teaching about Jewish courts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devarim from the man who once said he had no words. Your line was words come with time. Today, Moses remembers the judges he appointed.

A desk at a city office, two people in line. One is a well-known developer with a lawyer at his elbow and a building permit worth millions. The other is a retired woman whose neighbor's tree keeps dropping branches on her car. Whose file gets opened first? Whose gets read carefully? It isn't hard to guess how it often goes. Early in his farewell, Moses remembers setting up courts in the wilderness, and the charge he gave the judges. It's about exactly that line at that desk.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE IN LINE.` → `THE BIG FILE AND THE SMALL ONE.` → `MOSES CHARGES THE JUDGES.`

segments.voice: The charge, in the old Jewish translation, says: "ye shall hear the small and the great alike; ye shall not be afraid of the face of any man; for the judgment is God's." Three pieces. First, small and great alike. The rabbis took that literally, about money. In the Talmud, in Sanhedrin, Resh Lakish says a case over a single perutah, a tiny copper coin, must be as precious to the judge as a case over a hundred maneh, a fortune. Same care. Same patience. Same order in the line. Second, don't be afraid of the face of any man. A judge will someday face someone powerful, someone who could ruin them, someone with friends. The verse says: don't look away from the case to look at the face. And the reason is the third piece: the judgment is God's. Read that way, the judge isn't the owner of justice, just the one holding it for a while, and answerable for how it was held. Notice who is listening to this speech. Not judges, mostly. A whole people. Moses is retelling it to everyone, because everyone ends up judging something: whose complaint gets heard at work, which kid's version of the fight gets believed, whose message gets answered tonight and whose waits a week. The small and the great show up at all of those desks.
screen: `HEAR THE SMALL AND THE GREAT ALIKE.` · `A PENNY CASE, A FORTUNE CASE.` · `DON'T FEAR ANY FACE.` · `THE JUDGMENT IS GOD'S.` · then, large: `SMALL AND GREAT ALIKE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small worry someone brought you lately that you brushed past: a kid's question, a coworker's minor complaint, a parent's repeated story. Hold it up the way you'd hold a big one, and ask what they were really asking for. Let yourself feel the size it was to them.
Devarim. Words, the name of this last book, where Moses retells even the charge he gave the first judges.
Your line: small and great alike. A week of edges: a date remembered, a city of refuge, a land that's shared, the edge of the Jordan, and now the words. That's day four hundred eighty-three.
